---
title: "The Exact Size of the Conflict-Free Gadget Hierarchy"
subtitle: "A closed form and matching growth rate for $|G_k|$"
author: "Shrey Shah"
date: today
abstract: |
  Abel et al. (2018) construct a family of graphs $G_k$ with
  $\chi_{CF}(G_k) = k$, used as the forcing gadget in their proof that
  conflict-free coloring is NP-complete for every fixed $k \ge 3$. They bound
  the size of this family between $\Omega(2^k)$ and
  $\mathcal{O}(2^{k \log k})$. We give a closed form for $|G_k|$ by reducing
  the size recurrence to a Pell recurrence, and show
  $|G_k| = \Theta\!\left(k!\,(1+\sqrt{2})^{k}\right)$, with the normalized
  ratio $|G_k| / (k!\,\alpha^k)$ converging to an explicit constant. The rate
  is consistent with both published bounds and strictly sharper than either.

## Setup {#sec-setup}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Sections @sec-counting through @sec-comparison are reproduced verbatim from the
longer walkthrough. This section is the only new material, and exists to make
the note self-contained.
:::

We recall the two definitions the result depends on, and nothing else.

::: {#def-cf}

### Conflict-free coloring

A **partial $k$-coloring** of $G$ is an assignment $\chi : V' \to \{1, \dots, k\}$
for some subset $V' \subseteq V(G)$; vertices outside $V'$ are **uncolored**. Such a
$\chi$ is **conflict-free** with respect to closed neighborhoods if for every
$v \in V(G)$ there is a vertex $w \in N[v] \cap V'$ whose color is unique in $N[v]$ —
that is, $\chi(w') \neq \chi(w)$ for every other $w' \in N[v] \cap V'$. We call $w$ the
**conflict-free neighbor** of $v$. The **conflict-free chromatic number**
$\chi_{CF}(G)$ is the smallest $k$ for which such a coloring exists.
:::

The family $G_k$ is built recursively, with $G_1$ a single vertex and $G_2$ the
star $K_{1,3}$ with one edge subdivided. Given $G_k$ and $G_{k-1}$:

* Take a complete graph $G = K_{k+1}$ on $k+1$ vertices.
* To each vertex $v \in V(K_{k+1})$ attach two disjoint and independent copies of
  $G_k$, adding an edge from every $v$ to every vertex of both copies of $G_k$.
* For each edge $e = vw \in E(K_{k+1})$, add two disjoint and independent copies
  of $G_{k-1}$, where there is an edge from every $v$ and $w$ to every vertex on
  both copies of $G_{k-1}$.

This gives $\chi_{CF}(G_k) = k$ for all $k \ge 1$. Only the vertex counts matter
below.

## Counting the vertices {#sec-counting}

$$|G_1| = 1, \qquad |G_2| = 5, \qquad |G_3| = 3 + 3\big(2|G_2|\big) + 3\big(2|G_1|\big) = 3 + 30 + 6 = 39 .$$

In general, the core contributes $k+1$ vertices, each of the $k+1$ core vertices
carries $2|G_k|$, and each of the $\binom{k+1}{2}$ core edges carries
$2|G_{k-1}|$. Since

$$\binom{k+1}{2} = \frac{(k+1)!}{2!\,(k-1)!} = \frac{k(k+1)}{2},$$

we get

$$|G_{k+1}| \;=\; \underbrace{(k+1)}_{v \in K_{k+1}} \;+\; \underbrace{2(k+1)\,|G_k|}_{H \text{ graphs}} \;+\; \underbrace{k(k+1)\,|G_{k-1}|}_{J \text{ graphs}}$$

and factoring out $(k+1)$,

$$\boxed{\;|G_{k+1}| = (k+1)\Big(2|G_k| + k\,|G_{k-1}| + 1\Big).\;}$$

Check: $|G_3| = 3(2\cdot 5 + 2\cdot 1 + 1) = 3 \cdot 13 = 39$ and
$|G_4| = 4(2 \cdot 39 + 3 \cdot 5 + 1) = 4 \cdot 94 = 376$.

## Algorithmic bounds {#sec-bounds}

Every term of the bracket is positive, so $a_{k+1} \ge 2a_k$, and therefore

$$a_k = \Omega\!\left(2^k\right).$$

This is the bound stated in the paper, and it is all that is needed there. We can
do better by keeping the factor in front: since $a_{k+1} \ge 2(k+1)a_k$,
unrolling from $a_2 = 5$ gives

$$a_k \;\ge\; 5 \prod_{j=3}^{k} 2j \;=\; 5 \cdot 2^{k-2} \cdot \frac{k!}{2},$$

so $\log_2 a_k = \Omega(k \log k)$.

The sequence is increasing, so $a_{k-1} \le a_k$, and also $1 \le a_k$. Hence

$$a_{k+1} \;\le\; (k+1)\big(2a_k + k\,a_k + a_k\big) \;=\; (k+1)(k+3)\,a_k \;\le\; (k+3)^2 a_k .$$

Unrolling from $a_1 = 1$,

$$a_{k+1} \;\le\; \prod_{j=1}^{k} (j+3)^2 \;\le\; (k+3)^{2k},$$

and taking logarithms,

$$\log_2 a_{k+1} \;\le\; 2k \log_2 (k+3) \;=\; O(k \log k),$$

so $a_k = \mathcal{O}\!\left(2^{k \log k}\right)$.

### Solving the recurrence

First we rewrite our recurrence as a sequence:

$$a_1 = 1, \qquad a_2 = 5, \qquad a_{k+1} = (k+1)\big(2a_k + k\,a_{k-1} + 1\big), \qquad k, a \in \mathbb{Z}^+ .$$

The $(k+1)$ out front and the $k$ on the second term hide a Pell recurrence. We
divide it out.

## Normalizing away the factorials {#sec-normalizing}

Divide both sides by $(k+1)!$:

$$\frac{a_{k+1}}{(k+1)!} \;=\; \frac{2a_k + k\,a_{k-1} + 1}{k!} .$$

Let $b_k = \dfrac{a_k}{k!}$. The middle term simplifies because
$\dfrac{k\,a_{k-1}}{k!} = \dfrac{a_{k-1}}{(k-1)!} = b_{k-1}$, so

$$b_{k+1} \;=\; 2b_k + b_{k-1} + \frac{1}{k!} .$$

Isolating the $1/k!$, what is left is exactly the **Pell recurrence**

$$b_{k+1} = 2b_k + b_{k-1} .$$

The seeds come from the graph: $b_1 = \dfrac{a_1}{1!} = 1$, where $a_1$ is the
number of vertices in $G_1$, and $b_2 = \dfrac{a_2}{2!} = \dfrac{5}{2}$,
referencing $K_{1,3}$ for $a_2$.

## The Pell recurrence {#sec-pell}

$$P_n = 2P_{n-1} + P_{n-2}, \qquad P_0 = 0,\; P_1 = 1, \qquad \langle 0,1,2,5,12,29,70,\dots\rangle$$

Set $P_n = r^n$, so $r^n = 2r^{n-1} + r^{n-2}$, giving $r^2 = 2r + 1$ and

$$r^2 - 2r - 1 = 0, \qquad r = \frac{2 \pm \sqrt{4+4}}{2} = \frac{2 \pm \sqrt{8}}{2}, \qquad r = 1 + \sqrt{2},\; r = 1 - \sqrt{2}.$$

The recurrence is linear, so

$$P_n = A\big(1+\sqrt{2}\big)^n + B\big(1-\sqrt{2}\big)^n$$

where $A$ and $B$ satisfy all values of the recurrence. From $P_0 = 0$ we get
$A = -B$, and from $P_1 = 1$,

$$1 = A\big(1+\sqrt2\big) - A\big(1-\sqrt2\big) = A\big(1 + \sqrt2 + \sqrt2 - 1\big) = A \cdot 2\sqrt2 ,$$

so $A = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt2}$ and $B = \dfrac{-1}{2\sqrt2}$, giving

$$P_n = \frac{\big(1+\sqrt{2}\big)^n - \big(1-\sqrt{2}\big)^n}{2\sqrt{2}} .$$

### The homogeneous part

Running the Pell recurrence forward from $b_1, b_2$:

$$b_3 = 2b_2 + b_1, \qquad b_4 = 2b_3 + b_2 = 5b_2 + 2b_1, \qquad b_5 = 2b_4 + b_3 = 12b_2 + 5b_1 .$$

The coefficients are Pell numbers, so we generalize:

$$b_k \;=\; P_{k-1}\,b_2 + P_{k-2}\,b_1 \;=\; \frac{5}{2}P_{k-1} + P_{k-2} .$$

### The inhomogeneous part

Our actual recurrence has $1/k!$ added, so

$$b_3 = 6 + \frac{1}{2!} = 6.5, \qquad b_4 = 2b_3 + b_2 + \frac{1}{3!} = 5b_2 + 2b_1 + \frac{1}{3!} + 2\left(\frac{1}{2!}\right),$$

$$b_5 = 2b_4 + b_3 + \frac{1}{4!} = 12b_2 + 5b_1 + 2\left(\frac{1}{3!}\right) + 5\left(\frac{1}{2!}\right) + \frac{1}{4!} .$$

Each factorial creates its own Pell: a term $\dfrac{1}{j!}$ injected at step $j$
propagates forward with Pell coefficients, contributing $\dfrac{P_{k-j}}{j!}$ to
$b_k$.

*Verification.* Let $k = 5$, $j = 2$. We have $\dfrac{P_3}{2!}$, where $P_3 = 5$,
so $\dfrac{5}{2!}$ — which is the coefficient appearing on $\dfrac{1}{2!}$ in
$b_5$ above.

Accounting for every $j$, for some $k$:

$$\sum_{j=2}^{k-1} \frac{P_{k-j}}{j!} .$$

## The closed form {#sec-closed-form}

Solving for our altered Pell recurrence:

$$b_k \;=\; \frac{5P_{k-1}}{2} + P_{k-2} + \sum_{j=2}^{k-1} \frac{P_{k-j}}{j!} .$$

Remember that $b_k = \dfrac{a_k}{k!}$, and that $a_k$ is just our actual
recurrence sequentialized, so

$$\boxed{\;|G_k| \;=\; k!\left[\,P_{k-2} + \frac{5P_{k-1}}{2} + \sum_{j=2}^{k-1} \frac{P_{k-j}}{j!}\,\right]\;}$$

with $P_n$ as above. Using the standard backward extension $P_{-1} = 1$, this is
valid for all $k \ge 1$.

*Check.* $k = 3$ gives $6\left[2 + \tfrac52 + \tfrac{P_1}{2!}\right] = 6(6.5) = 39$,
and $k = 4$ gives $24\left[5 + \tfrac{25}{2} + \tfrac{P_2}{2!} + \tfrac{P_1}{3!}\right] = 24\left(\tfrac{47}{3}\right) = 376$,
matching the direct counts. The sequence continues
$1,\,5,\,39,\,376,\,4545,\,65826,\,1112461,\dots$

## Growth rate {#sec-growth}

Write $\alpha = 1+\sqrt2$ and $\beta = 1-\sqrt2$, so

$$P_n = \frac{\alpha^n - \beta^n}{2\sqrt2} .$$

Since $|\beta| = \sqrt2 - 1 < 1$, the $\beta^n$ term vanishes and

$$\lim_{n \to \infty} P_n = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{\alpha^n}{2\sqrt2}, \qquad\text{so}\qquad P_n = \Theta\!\left(\alpha^n\right) = \Theta\!\left(\big(1+\sqrt2\big)^n\right).$$

For the sum, $P_{k-j} = \Theta\!\left(\alpha^{k-j}\right)$, so

$$\sum_{j=2}^{k-1} \frac{P_{k-j}}{j!} \;=\; \Theta\!\left(\sum_{j=2}^{k-1} \frac{\alpha^{k}}{j!\,\alpha^{j}}\right) \;=\; \Theta\!\left(\alpha^{k} \sum_{j=2}^{k-1} \frac{1}{j!\,\alpha^{j}}\right),$$

where $\sum_{j\ge2} \dfrac{1}{j!\,\alpha^{j}}$ converges — to $e^{1/\alpha} - 1 - \tfrac{1}{\alpha}$ —
so the whole sum is $\Theta\!\left(\alpha^k\right)$. (The $j=2$ term alone is
already $\Theta(\alpha^k)$, which gives the matching lower bound.)

The remaining pieces $\dfrac{5P_{k-1}}{2}$ and $P_{k-2}$ are Pell recurrences
multiplied by the constants $\dfrac{5}{2\alpha}$ and $\dfrac{1}{\alpha^2}$
respectively, so they are both $\Theta\!\left(\alpha^k\right)$ as well.

So $\dfrac{|G_k|}{k!} = \Theta\!\left(\big(1+\sqrt2\big)^k\right)$, and thus

$$\boxed{\;|G_k| \;=\; \Theta\!\left(k!\,\big(1+\sqrt{2}\big)^{k}\right).\;}$$

Because every piece has the same growth constant, the ratio actually converges
rather than merely being bounded:

$$\lim_{k\to\infty} \frac{|G_k|}{k!\,\alpha^k} \;=\; \frac{1}{2\sqrt2}\left(e^{\sqrt2 - 1} + \frac{1-\sqrt2}{2}\right) \;\approx\; 0.4617667 ,$$

using $1/\alpha = \sqrt2 - 1$.

## Comparison with the paper {#sec-comparison}

The paper states only that $|G_k|$ is in $\Omega\!\left(2^k\right)$ and
$\mathcal{O}\!\left(2^{k \log k}\right)$, for
**fixed** $k$ the gadget has constant size, which is what makes the reduction in
Lemma 3.4 run in polynomial time. The exact rate is consistent with both bounds,
since $\log_2\!\left(k!\,\alpha^k\right) = \Theta(k \log k)$, but the closed form derived in this document along with it's growth raate are strictly
sharper because we pin the base at $1 + \sqrt2 \approx 2.414$

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**What the sharper rate buys.** The constant hidden in the reduction of
[@abel2018, Lemma 3.4] is $C_1 = 2|G_k|$. Under the closed form this is
$\Theta\!\left(k!\,(1+\sqrt2)^k\right)$, already $752$ at $k = 4$. The reduction
is therefore linear for each fixed $k$ and catastrophic in $k$, which is why the
result is a statement about CF $k$-Coloring for each constant $k$ rather than
about the problem with $k$ given as part of the input.
:::
